channel.title: The Missing Seat
channel.description: Evidence-based editorials asking who is missing, why it matters, and what can be done.

item.title: The Complaint Had a 100-Day Clock. The Housing Problem Did Not Wait.
item.description: HUD now claims a 46% fair-housing backlog reduction. The starting counts, cases still waiting and relief delivered belong in the public receipt.

item.title: A Seat Was Made: Timor-Leste Kept Showing Up Until Disease Lost Ground.
item.description: Timor-Leste's disease-elimination milestones deserve attention for the public work behind them. The next accountability question is how that protection will be maintained.

item.title: The College Took the Money. The Outcome Data Is Late.
item.description: Students must choose, sign and borrow on time. Required college program data is still arriving late.

item.title: The Gap Is Not Just Pay. It Is Who Gets Time, Care, and Power.
item.description: Women are nearly half of employed America. Pay, promotion, unpaid care and access to leadership need a fuller workforce receipt.

item.title: The Disability Hiring Duty Stayed. The Audits Stopped.
item.description: Federal contractors still owe disabled workers equal opportunity. GAO says the Labor Department suspended the audits used to test that promise.

item.title: Germany Has a Way to Keep the Power On. Can People Use It?
item.description: Germany's energy law offers eligible basic-supply households a way to prevent disconnection through interest-free repayment and continued supply.

item.title: He Asked to Break His Fast. He Allegedly Lost His Job.
item.description: A coffee-shop settlement raises a practical question about religious freedom at work: can an employee request a workable schedule without risking the income that keeps them afloat?

item.title: Before You Cut Care, Did You Stop Paying More for the Same Care?
item.description: Before Washington saves money by reducing coverage or enrollment, did it exhaust the billions available from paying the same rate for comparable outpatient care?

item.title: Germany Created a Seat for Police Complaints. Who Can Actually Use It?
item.description: Germany's federal police commissioner received 421 submissions in one year, including 50 reporting concrete indications of discrimination or racial profiling. The office is real. So are the limits on who can use it.

item.title: They Served the Country. The Food Benefit Still Missed Them.
item.description: An average of 1.4 million veterans faced food insecurity each year from 2015 through 2020. A new federal review found that outdated outreach and a slowed federal hand-off may keep eligible veterans from using SNAP.

item.title: Two Agencies Fund the Support. The Worker Still Gets Left Waiting.
item.description: A new federal review describes gaps between disability employment programs. The person trying to work should not have to become the coordinator of the government meant to support them.

item.title: Learning to Unlearn
item.description: We inherit more than property and money. We inherit explanations. Some deserve to be kept. Some need to be unlearned.

item.title: The Warning Arrived. The Language Did Not.
item.description: A warning is not truly public if millions of people cannot understand it. Federal weather alerts remain uneven across languages, while a promising translation project still lacks measurable goals, a complete resource plan and nationwide reach.

item.title: She Was Qualified to Repair the Pallets. The Company Allegedly Only Hired Men.
item.description: A pallet-repair settlement opens a larger question: how much of what we still call “men’s work” reflects actual job requirements, and how much survives because employers keep treating sex as a qualification?

item.title: She Was Qualified to Repair the Pallets. The Company Allegedly Only Hired Men.
item.description: A pallet-repair settlement opens a larger question: how much of what we still call men’s work reflects actual job requirements, and how much survives because employers keep treating sex as a qualification?

item.title: The Cloud Has an Address. Somebody Else Is Paying the Bill.
item.description: AI feels weightless on a screen. The data centers behind it need electricity, water, land and infrastructure. The public deserves to know who gets the benefit and who carries the risk.

item.title: You Can Talk About Racism and Still Be Happy
item.description: Remembering slavery, segregation and racism is not inherited guilt. A country can move forward without pretending its darkest history left nothing behind.

item.title: The Absurdity of Being Black in America
item.description: America asks Black people to trust its promises. What happens when institutions won’t answer what their own decisions left behind?

item.title: America Keeps Measuring Black Anger. Who Is Measuring Black Strength?
item.description: America scrutinizes Black anger. It should also examine the strength it takes to keep going, the psychological cost, and the support still missing.

item.title: The Disaster Plan Included Everyone. The Training for Disability Access Disappeared.
item.description: FEMA removed disability-inclusion training for its state and local partners, did not consistently coordinate specialists before disasters, and had never asked people with disabilities to evaluate the overall assistance application process.

item.title: The Absence Rate Was Over 100%. The Oversight Had Already Stopped.
item.description: At least one in four students has been chronically absent. But the federal data used to track the problem can produce rates above 100 percent, and the Education Department stopped its most comprehensive oversight of the programs carrying nearly $27 billion.

item.title: The Water Project Was Built. The Missing Money Was for Keeping It Alive.
item.description: Washington likes to cut the ribbon when a water system is built. A new federal audit shows what happens when the rules do not cover every home and the money to keep the system working is treated as somebody else’s problem.

item.title: The Efficiency Team Got Access. The Public Still Cannot See the Security Receipt.
item.description: GAO could not verify the full access or safeguards because six agencies supplied incomplete records. This is an assurance gap, not proof of a breach.

item.title: The HR Manager Said No to Discrimination. Then She Allegedly Lost Her Job.
item.description: An equal-opportunity policy means little if the person expected to defend it can be punished for speaking.

item.title: They Served the United States. The Nearest VA Care May Be an Ocean Away.
item.description: Citizens of three Pacific nations can enlist in the U.S. military. But after they return home, VA healthcare may require an international flight without VA travel reimbursement.

item.title: They Trusted Black Women With Their Babies. Just Not With Power.
item.description: America trusted Black women with intimate responsibilities, including caring for white children. But trust in their labor did not become equal protection, fair pay or equal power.

item.title: The Campaign Was the Ad. We’re Stuck With the Bill.
item.description: American candidates can promise tax cuts, new programs and sweeping savings without giving voters one independent receipt for the whole plan. Australia already shows that another way is possible.

item.title: Trump and Black America: What Helped, What Hurt, and What Will Last?
item.description: A plain-language ledger of what changed, who gained, who lost, what is temporary, what is law, and whether the Black-white gap actually narrowed.

item.title: Dear World: Before You Tell Me How Great America Is, Tell the Whole Story
item.description: America can celebrate what it built without hiding who paid for it. If the world wants to understand this country, it has to meet all of us, not just the America in the commercial.

item.title: The Robe Doesn’t Erase What the Judge Knows
item.description: A judge’s recorded prejudice raises a question retirement alone cannot answer: What happened in the cases she already decided?

item.title: “Black-on-Black Crime”: Naming the Violence Without Hiding Its History
item.description: Violence within Black communities is real. So is the history that shaped where violence, poverty and disadvantage became concentrated.

item.title: What Can We Do to Make Justice Happen?
item.description: If injustice was built through laws, institutions and public choices, what can be done now?

item.title: The Class Construction After Reconstruction
item.description: Emancipation ended slavery. It did not erase the economic and social hierarchy built around it.

item.title: Nigger: The Word, the Law and the Line We Draw
item.description: The public often punishes America’s most infamous racial slur more readily than the hierarchy the word declares.

item.title: Power Is Not Proof of Superiority
item.description: Centuries of oppression prove that domination can be organized and preserved. They do not prove a racial hierarchy.

item.title: The Violence Behind the Reconstruction Amendments
item.description: The doctrine cannot be separated from the murders, rape, torture, massacres and political terror that constitutional protection was meant to confront.
